claims.claim: scikit-learn's StandardScaler stores mean_ and scale_ after fit.
claims.source: scikit-learn 1.8 API reference; checked in this repository's dev environment.

concept_html:
Python does not require classes. Many data science classes are functions in disguise: an __init__ that stores arguments, and one method that uses them.

class Normaliser:
    def __init__(self, col):
        self.col = col

    def run(self, df):
        return df.assign(**{self.col: df[self.col] / df[self.col].sum()})

Every caller writes Normaliser("spend").run(df). A function, normalise(df, col), says the same thing in one call, with nothing to construct.

A class earns its place when at least one of these holds:

  • State that outlives one call. A weighting model learns targets in fit and applies them in transform. scikit-learn's StandardScaler stores mean_ and scale_ between the two calls.
  • An invariant to protect. A Weights object guarantees values are positive and sum to the sample size. Code that builds one through its constructor cannot break that rule.
  • Several operations on the same data. A SurveyDesign with mean(), ci() and subgroup() that all need weights, strata and clusters.
  • A shared interface. Several classes with the same method, such as load(), so the caller swaps one for another.

Settings with no behaviour belong in a dataclass (lesson B2-L2). A single step belongs in a function (lesson B2-L1).

Test a design by asking: if you delete the class and keep its methods as functions, what breaks? If nothing, keep the functions.

code_lines: class Deduper:
def __init__(self) -> None:
self.seen: set[int] = set()
def run(self, ids: list[int]) -> list[int]:
out = [i for i in ids if i not in self.seen]
self.seen.update(ids)
return out
d = Deduper()
d.run([1, 2, 3])
print(d.run([2, 3, 4]))

solution_lines: import pandas as pd
def add_share(df: pd.DataFrame, col: str) -> pd.DataFrame:
"""Return df with share = col / column total, or 0.0 when the total is zero."""
total = df[col].sum()
return df.assign(share=0.0)
return df.assign(share=df[col] / total)

code_lines: class Scaler:
"""Standardise with the mean and sd learned in fit."""
def fit(self, values: list[float]) -> "Scaler":
n = len(values)
self.mean_ = sum(values) / n
self.sd_ = (sum((v - self.mean_) ** 2 for v in values) / n) ** 0.5
return self
def transform(self, values: list[float]) -> list[float]:
self.fit(values)
return [(v - self.mean_) / self.sd_ for v in values]

title: When a class earns its place
why_html:
A team wraps each cleaning step in a class: DropDuplicates, FixDates, RenameColumns, each with __init__ and run. A new analyst adds a self.seen_ids set to DropDuplicates to speed up a second call. The pipeline object is reused across two tracker waves, so wave 2 silently drops every respondent who also took part in wave 1: 38% of the sample.

Pure functions have no self to keep stale state between calls.
